Abstract— The rise of the low-altitude economy (LAE) is
propelling urban development and emerging industries by inte-
grating advanced technologies to enhance efficiency, safety, and
sustainability in low-altitude operations. The widespread adop-
tion of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) and electric vertical
takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft plays a crucial role in
enabling key applications within LAE, such as urban logis-
tics, emergency rescue, and aerial mobility. However, unlike
traditional UAV networks, LAE networks encounter increased
airspace management demands due to dense flying nodes
and potential interference with ground communication systems.

In addition, there are heightened and extended security risks
in real-time operations, particularly the vulnerability of low-
altitude aircraft to cyberattacks from ground-based threats.
To address these, this paper first explores related standards and
core architecture that support the development of LAE networks.
Subsequently, we highlight the integration of technologies such
as communication, sensing, computing, positioning, navigation,
surveillance, flight control, and airspace management. We also
analyze how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) contributes
to this integration by enabling intelligent adaptation, uncer-
tainty modeling, and real-time optimization. This synergy of
multi-technology drives the advancement of real-world LAE
applications, particularly in improving operational efficiency,
optimizing airspace usage, and ensuring safety. Finally, we outline
future research directions for LAE networks, such as intelligent
and adaptive optimization, security and privacy protection,
sustainable energy and power management, quantum-driven
coordination, generative governance, and three-dimensional (3D)
airspace coverage, which collectively underscore the potential of
collaborative technologies to advance LAE networks.
Index Terms— Low-altitude economy (LAE) networks,
uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), electric vertical takeoff and
landing (eVTOL), generative artificial intelligence (GAI),
multi-technology integration.

many regions are facing increasingly serious chal-
lenges, such as shortages of computational resources and
inefficiencies in system performance. For example, the grow-
ing complexity of ground transportation systems leads to
network congestion, reduced positioning accuracy, and over-
loaded computational resources, thus affecting the efficiency
and responsiveness of urban operations [1]. At the same
time, logistics in suburban and remote areas encounters even
more complex issues, such as inconvenient transportation, high
costs, and poor timeliness, which severely hamper the flow
of goods and emergency response capabilities [2]. In this

enabled systems have made progress [3], [4], [5], [6], [7],
[8], [9], [10], they still face significant barriers in regulation,

I. INTRODUCTION

many regions are facing increasingly serious chal-
lenges, such as shortages of computational resources and

ing complexity of ground transportation systems leads to

[8], [9], [10], they still face significant barriers in regulation,

effectively meet the multi-layered demands of cross-regional
and complex environments, and they are unable to coordinate
and provide sustainable services in high-density airspace and
resource-constrained areas. Therefore, there is an urgent need
for an innovative, green, and intelligent solution that can
overcome these limitations. The solution can facilitate more
efficient, flexible, and sustainable technologies to drive long-
term development across various sectors.

As an emerging industrial form, the low-altitude econ-
omy (LAE) provides a highly effective solution to current
challenges by leveraging their significant potential advan-
tages. Specifically, by unlocking the underutilized strategic
airspace between 500 and 3000 meters above the ground
and integrating dynamic management with layered operational
models, LAE significantly enhances airspace efficiency and
flexibility. Moreover, the electric vertical take-off and landing
(eVTOL) aircraft [12] represent a rapidly advancing class
of aerial vehicles that utilize electric propulsion systems for
vertical take-off, hovering, and landing. Unlike conventional
aircraft, they typically employ distributed electric propulsion
systems, which eliminate the need for runways and offer
advantages such as low noise, simplified structures, and sys-
tem redundancy. These characteristics make them especially
suitable for operations in low-altitude airspace. Furthermore,
breakthroughs in hydrogen-powered propulsion systems [13]
and distributed thrust technologies [14] support aircraft with
extended range and reduced dependence on traditional fuel
sources. In addition, using shared airspace (e.g., the layered
operation of logistics aircraft alongside crewed aircraft) and
reusable infrastructure (e.g., rooftop landing platforms that
double as logistics hubs), the LAE ensures efficient use
of resources. Furthermore, generative artificial intelligence
(GAI) technology has been applied to the optimization of
communication and beamforming in LAE networks, which
demonstrates the potential of GAI to enhance operational
performance and system robustness [15], [16]. Given these

Multi-Technology Integration for Low-Altitude Applications (Section IV), and Future Directions for Collaborative Technologies in LAE Networks (Section V).
As an emerging industrial form, the low-altitude econ-
omy (LAE) provides a highly effective solution to current
challenges by leveraging their significant potential advan-
tages. Specifically, by unlocking the underutilized strategic
airspace between 500 and 3000 meters above the ground
and integrating dynamic management with layered operational
models, LAE significantly enhances airspace efficiency and
flexibility. Moreover, the electric vertical take-off and landing
(eVTOL) aircraft [12] represent a rapidly advancing class
of aerial vehicles that utilize electric propulsion systems for
vertical take-off, hovering, and landing. Unlike conventional
aircraft, they typically employ distributed electric propulsion
systems, which eliminate the need for runways and offer
advantages such as low noise, simplified structures, and sys-
tem redundancy. These characteristics make them especially
suitable for operations in low-altitude airspace. Furthermore,
breakthroughs in hydrogen-powered propulsion systems [13]
and distributed thrust technologies [14] support aircraft with
extended range and reduced dependence on traditional fuel
sources. In addition, using shared airspace (e.g., the layered
operation of logistics aircraft alongside crewed aircraft) and
reusable infrastructure (e.g., rooftop landing platforms that
double as logistics hubs), the LAE ensures efficient use
of resources. Furthermore, generative artificial intelligence
(GAI) technology has been applied to the optimization of
communication and beamforming in LAE networks, which
demonstrates the potential of GAI to enhance operational
performance and system robustness [15], [16]. Given these
advantages, LAE demonstrates broad application potential in
various sectors, such as logistics, rescue, transportation, and
inspection. In addition to fostering diverse applications, LAE
also drives innovation in UAVs [17], [18], [19], artificial
intelligence (AI) [20], [21], and other technologies [22], [23],
[24], [25]. This will further promote the upgrade of high-tech
industries and lay the foundation for the digital transformation
of the economy [26].

also drives innovation in UAVs [17], [18], [19], artificial

of the economy [26].
However, fully unleashing the potential of LAE and
enabling its widespread applications require the development
of efficient LAE networks, which must meet several key
requirements and overcome practical challenges.
Key Requirements: These are essential to enable stable and
efficient low-altitude operations.
• Intelligent autonomous decision-making capabilities are
crucial [27]. This can be achieved through the deep
integration of communication, sensing, and computing,
which create a real-time environmental sensing and
adaptive response system, thereby allowing aircraft to
autonomously avoid risks and optimize flight paths in
complex airspace.
• A high-precision collaborative technology system is fun-
damental for efficient operations [28]. This requires
the collaboration of multi-modal sensors, anti-jamming
navigation, and real-time aircraft monitoring to ensure
centimeter-level positioning accuracy, millisecond-level
response times, and safe operations in dense airspace.
• An elastic resource scheduling mechanism is key to
optimizing operational efficiency [29]. By leveraging
dynamic data analysis and digital twin (DT) modeling,
an intelligent scheduling system can respond to changes
in logistics demand or weather conditions, further enhanc-
ing airspace utilization and energy efficiency.
• Effective dynamic airspace management is essential [30].
This involves developing an intelligent air traffic man-
agement system that supports the collaborative operation
of heterogeneous aircraft. The system should incorpo-
rate dynamic airspace allocation algorithms and conflict
prediction models for seamless coordination between
crewed aircraft, logistics UAVs, and ground trans-
portation, while also maintaining compatibility with
international airspace management standards.
Practical Challenges: Several issues still hinder large-scale
deployment and coordination.
• Fragmented regulatory systems, inconsistent approval
procedures, and the lack of standardized low-altitude
traffic rules may hinder the coordination of airspace, com-
munication, and service layers, thereby limiting cross-
regional operations of low-altitude aircraft. Moreover,
ambiguity in data privacy and compliance governance for
aerial operations further impedes large-scale deployment.
• Managing spectrum usage and mitigating interference
is particularly challenging due to the shared or unli-
censed frequency bands used by low-altitude aircraft,
edge devices, and ground stations, which is further com-
plicated by the high mobility of aerial platforms.
• Dense urban environments introduce severe signal degra-
dation caused by obstructions, multipath effects, and
frequent non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions, which can
compromise communication, localization, and sensing,
especially in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-
denied scenarios.
• Environmental uncertainties such as rain, fog, snow, and
turbulence can affect aircraft stability, communication
link quality, and task execution efficiency. Unlike fixed
ground infrastructure, low-altitude aircraft are highly
exposed to atmospheric disturbances, imposing stricter
demands on control and perception systems.
Based on the above challenges, this survey focuses on the
multidimensional synergy of supporting technologies and the
key challenges they face. These include the integration of
communication, sensing, and intelligent computing, collabora-
tion of positioning, navigation, and surveillance, and fusion of
flight control with airspace management. Moreover, GAI plays
a vital role in this synergistic process in terms of intelligent
adaptation, uncertainty modeling, and real-time optimization.

spans.content: A. Related Works and Contributions
Given the popularity of LAE, several surveys have estab-
lished a solid foundation for understanding the related
technologies and applications. Table II
summarizes these
surveys and shows the distinct contributions of our own
survey.
In [31], a low-altitude intelligent transportation (LAIT)
system framework based on a cyber-physical system (CPS)
architecture was proposed, along with a lifecycle management
framework to improve the efficiency of low-altitude traffic
operations. Moreover, the authors emphasized innovations in
key technologies such as UAVs, AI, internet of things (IoT),
6G, cloud computing, and blockchain, which demonstrate the
broad technological basis supporting LAE networks. Mean-
while, several surveys have explored the emerging role of GAI
in enhancing specific domains. In [32], the authors surveyed
the role of GAI in securing physical-layer communica-
tions, including confidentiality, authentication, and robustness.
In addition, [33] offered a comprehensive review of GAI for
physical-layer signal processing, highlighting its advantages
in tasks such as channel estimation, modulation recognition,
and equalization. Furthermore, [34] investigated a GAI-driven
semantic communication framework that underscores infor-
mation regeneration over traditional decoding, while [35]
examined semantic transmission, knowledge modeling, and
resource management. Despite these valuable contributions,
these surveys focus on individual technological aspects and
do not delve into how these technologies can be seamlessly
integrated and synergized, which is critical for the comprehen-
sive development of LAE networks.
In contrast to the above efforts, a new wave of research has
emerged that integrates GAI across multiple submodules to
support LAE-level coordination. For example, [36] provided
an extensive survey on intelligent integrated sensing and com-
munication (ISAC), outlining how AI incorporation enhances
system adaptability and reduces reliance on explicit modeling.
Moreover, [37] addressed the challenges of swarm intelligence
in uncrewed vehicle networks and discussed how GAI can
facilitate collaborative perception and decision-making among
multiple agents. Furthermore, [27] explored how embodied
artificial intelligence (EAI) can be utilized to achieve the inte-
gration of sensing, communication, computation, and control
(ISC3) for LAE scenarios. Additionally, [38] proposed the
integrated sensing, communication, and computation (ISCC)
framework, which provides a holistic solution for multi-
resource orchestration and task-aware collaboration in future
edge-intelligent networks. However, the aforementioned sur-
veys predominantly emphasize communication, sensing, and
computing technologies, while underestimating the essential
roles of navigation, positioning, surveillance, flight control,
and airspace management.
Different from existing surveys and tutorials, our survey
distinguishes itself by focusing specifically on the core tech-
nological architecture and applications of LAE networks.
Moreover, this survey offers a unique perspective by deeply
integrating communication, sensing, intelligent computing,
positioning, navigation, flight control, and airspace manage-
ment technologies. In particular, we highlight the enabling
role of GAI in enhancing system coordination and adaptability
under dynamic conditions. Therefore, this survey fills a gap
in the literature by thoroughly exploring how the synergy
of these technologies enables efficient and secure operations
in LAE networks, and by emphasizing their critical role
in addressing challenges such as aircraft coordination and
airspace management in complex airspace scenarios.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows:
• We highlight the distinctive features of LAE networks
compared to traditional UAV networks and describe the
multi-layer architecture that supports their development.
This establishes a technical framework for understanding
and evaluating LAE implementations.

spans.content: • We explore how the deep integration of communication,
sensing, intelligent computing, positioning, navigation,
surveillance, flight control, and airspace management
technologies drives the efficient and safe operation of
LAE networks. We also analyze how GAI contributes
to this integration by enabling intelligent adaptation,
uncertainty modeling, and real-time optimization. These
capabilities support emerging applications such as logis-
tics, rescue, transportation, and inspection.
• We outline future research directions for LAE net-
works, including intelligent and adaptive optimization,
security and privacy protection, sustainable energy and
power management, quantum-driven coordination, gen-
erative governance, and three-dimensional (3D) airspace
coverage. These discussions provide insights into how
collaborative technologies can meet future operational
needs in LAE systems.

presents the vision for LAE networks and its core architecture.
Section III provides an overview of the core technologies
supporting LAE networks. Section IV explores the multi-
technology integration in real-world applications. Section V
discusses the future research directions, and Section VI con-
cludes the paper. To aid the reader, Table I provides a list of
acronyms for quick reference, and Table III presents a glossary
of key terms to enhance conceptual clarity.

networks. Subsequently, we present the core architecture that
supports the development and operations of LAE networks.
A. Visions Toward LAE Networks
LAE networks have driven significant advancements in UAV
networks, which impose increasing demands on scalability,
efficiency, and reliability. By integrating multifunctional sys-
tems and enabling autonomous collaboration, LAE networks
achieve highly efficient operations. The following outlines the
key aspects of the developmental vision for LAE networks and
the standards that support them. In addition, Table IV presents
a comparison of relevant standards to support systematic
understanding and implementation.
1) Massive Connectivity: Enabling Large-Scale UAV Oper-
ations: Traditional UAV networks are typically capable of
efficiently supporting only a few dozen UAVs. When this
number is exceeded, issues such as signal interference and
communication disruptions often arise, which fail to meet the
demands of the performance in terms of real-time, flexibility,
and reliability [39]. This is primarily due to the limitations of
existing communication protocols and wireless resource man-
agement in high-density networks, including frequent channel
switching causing interruptions and instability in communi-
cation links, and inefficient spectrum management leading to
over-utilization or under-utilization of resources [40]. How-
ever, LAE networks need to support the coordinated operation
of hundreds or even thousands of UAVs, which places greater
demands on communication link stability, efficient spectrum
utilization, and effective route management.
To support such large-scale connectivity, the IEEE
1939.1-2021 standard [41] introduces new technologies that
collectively form a structured and scalable low-altitude
airspace framework. Specifically, the standard clearly defines
communication link quality requirements and network secu-
rity standards to ensure stable communications in dense
environments, and it also optimizes the low-altitude airspace
structure and flight route design through communication cov-
erage tests in the target airspace. Moreover, the standard
proposes a grid-based route planning method, which divides
the airspace into 1 km × 1 km grids and plans independent
flight paths within each grid to support the coordinated
operation of multiple UAVs. Furthermore, the standard inte-
grates enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) and ultra-reliable
low-latency communication (URLLC), thereby guaranteeing
reliable performance in high-communication-load scenarios
through dynamic frequency adjustment and real-time adapt-
ability. In addition, 3GPP Release-18 specifies new radio
(NR)-UAV enhancements,1 including UAV mobility manage-
ment, network slicing, and interference mitigation, which
further improve the scalability and robustness of UAV con-
nectivity.

A. Visions Toward LAE Networks
LAE networks have driven significant advancements in UAV
networks, which impose increasing demands on scalability,
efficiency, and reliability. By integrating multifunctional sys-
tems and enabling autonomous collaboration, LAE networks
achieve highly efficient operations. The following outlines the
key aspects of the developmental vision for LAE networks and
the standards that support them. In addition, Table IV presents
a comparison of relevant standards to support systematic
understanding and implementation.
1) Massive Connectivity: Enabling Large-Scale UAV Oper-
ations: Traditional UAV networks are typically capable of
efficiently supporting only a few dozen UAVs. When this
number is exceeded, issues such as signal interference and
communication disruptions often arise, which fail to meet the
demands of the performance in terms of real-time, flexibility,
and reliability [39]. This is primarily due to the limitations of
existing communication protocols and wireless resource man-
agement in high-density networks, including frequent channel
switching causing interruptions and instability in communi-
cation links, and inefficient spectrum management leading to
over-utilization or under-utilization of resources [40]. How-
ever, LAE networks need to support the coordinated operation
of hundreds or even thousands of UAVs, which places greater
demands on communication link stability, efficient spectrum
utilization, and effective route management.

1939.1-2021 standard [41] introduces new technologies that
collectively form a structured and scalable low-altitude
airspace framework. Specifically, the standard clearly defines
communication link quality requirements and network secu-
rity standards to ensure stable communications in dense
environments, and it also optimizes the low-altitude airspace
structure and flight route design through communication cov-
erage tests in the target airspace. Moreover, the standard
proposes a grid-based route planning method, which divides
the airspace into 1 km × 1 km grids and plans independent
flight paths within each grid to support the coordinated
operation of multiple UAVs. Furthermore, the standard inte-
grates enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) and ultra-reliable
low-latency communication (URLLC), thereby guaranteeing
reliable performance in high-communication-load scenarios
through dynamic frequency adjustment and real-time adapt-
ability. In addition, 3GPP Release-18 specifies new radio
(NR)-UAV enhancements,1 including UAV mobility manage-
ment, network slicing, and interference mitigation, which
further improve the scalability and robustness of UAV con-
nectivity.
2) Seamless Coordination: Integrating Core Capabilities for
Improved Efficiency: In traditional UAV networks, functions
such as sensing, navigation, communication, and control often
operate independently rather than being effectively coordi-
nated. For example, the sensing module collects environmental
data by using thermal imaging cameras, light detection and
ranging (LiDAR), or gas sensors [42], which is then trans-

operate independently rather than being effectively coordi-
nated. For example, the sensing module collects environmental
data by using thermal imaging cameras, light detection and
ranging (LiDAR), or gas sensors [42], which is then trans-
mitted by the communication module to a ground control
center for processing [43]. Subsequently, the navigation mod-
ule adjusts the flight path based on the returned results.
This multi-step interaction increases the data transmission
delays and limits the real-time task performance, especially in
complex and dynamic scenarios. In contrast, LAE networks
require seamless integration of these functions into a unified
framework to enable real-time data exchange and efficient task
optimization.
To make this possible, the IEEE 1937.8-2024 standard [44]
proposes the seamless integration of these key functions
through the coordinated operation of cellular communica-
tion terminals and other modules. In particular, the cellular
communication terminal, as the core module of the UAV,
supports beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) flight con-
trol and real-time transmission of high-definition video data.
Moreover, it is also responsible for collecting, processing, and
transmitting flight data (e.g., position, speed, and attitude)
and the task payload data (e.g., video streams and sensor
information). By interacting with ground control centers, the
terminal enables the real-time execution of flight commands,
as well as precise path planning and navigation. In addition,
to ensure efficient data transmission, the standard specifies the
use of both serial and Ethernet interfaces, with a requirement
that the switching delay of cellular base stations must not
exceed 5 milliseconds to maintain continuous communication.
Moreover, ITU-T Y.44212 defines a functional architecture for
UAV-controller interaction, coordinated communication, task
orchestration, and service management in complex network
environments.

cient Operations: Traditional UAV networks heavily rely on
human intervention, which requires ground operators to handle
task planning, path adjustments, and fault management [11].
This dependency leads to a lack of autonomy in adapting to
dynamic environments and unforeseen situations. Moreover,
task execution is often decentralized, with UAVs lacking
coordination mechanisms and information sharing [45], which
result in low resource utilization and diminish the effectiveness
of task completion. The LAE networks can address the above-
mentioned issues by incorporating AI into the UAV systems,

To better integrate AGI and enable efficient operations of
UAV swarms, the P1954 standard [50] defines an architecture
and protocol that support self-organizing and spectrum-flexible
communication for UAVs, which allows them to automatically
establish networks, dynamically adapt spectrum resources, and
maintain connections with ground users and devices. The
core components include dynamic network deployment, self-
organizing spectrum management functions, and integration
with existing communication standards such as the IEEE
P1900 series. This makes it applicable to disaster emergency
communications and the coordination of high-density UAV
swarms. In addition, the standard incorporates air-to-air com-
munication specifications from IEEE P1920.1 [51], along with
the dynamic spectrum access and interference co-existence
analysis from the IEEE 1900 series, thereby ensuring the
reliability and efficiency of communication.
4) Reliable Operations: Ensuring UAV Network Safety for
Critical Tasks: Critical tasks such as air taxi services, emer-
gency response, and medical supply transport place high
demands on the reliability and safety of UAV networks [52],
[53], [54]. However, traditional UAV networks rely on limited
communication links for redundant systems, and the adapt-
ability of multi-path technologies is often insufficient due
to technical constraints [55]. As a result, UAVs are more
prone to communication disruptions or data loss when facing
signal interference, network congestion, or other unforeseen
events, which can impact task execution and even cause task
failure [56]. Therefore, to ensure the reliable operation of
critical tasks in LAE networks, relevant standards provide
comprehensive specifications for flight supervision data trans-
mission and short message transmission protocols.
The IEEE 1937.3-2024 standard [57] specifies the content
of UAV flight monitoring data, including information such as
identity, status, latitude, longitude, altitude, heading, speed,
and timestamps. Moreover, it also mandates that the data
sampling interval does not exceed 2 seconds to ensure real-
time monitoring of UAV flight safety, so that the accurate
positioning and behavior tracking can be enabled. Further-
more, the standard utilizes the short message mechanism of the
GNSS, which defines the transmission and reception protocols
for flight supervision data and specifies the format for the
header and data sections of the data packets. In addition,
the immunity of this standard to space, territory, or terrain
limitations effectively enhances the continuity and stability of
flight supervision data transmission. Complementarily, ITU-
R M.21713 offers guidance on UAV spectrum requirements,
coexistence strategies, and interference evaluation to support
reliable and coordinated aerial operations.
B. Architecture of LAE Networks
To achieve efficient operation of low-altitude aircraft, a well-
designed architecture is essential. This architecture supports
both system stability and scalability, while facilitating seam-
less collaboration among its components. Specifically, the
details of the overall LAE network architecture are as fol-
lows. Moreover, an interaction diagram of the architecture is
provided, as shown in Fig. 2.
1) Airborne Terminal and Physical Infrastructure Layer:
The first layer of the LAE network architecture consists of
airborne terminals that are related to the aircraft manufacturing
and low-altitude physical infrastructure. Specifically, the for-
mer is a crucial component of the aircraft and plays a decisive
role in flight performance, safety, and reliability, and the latter
focuses on building a robust physical infrastructure to support
efficient low-altitude aviation operations.
Airborne Terminal: The airborne terminal provides the
foundation for power support, flight control, environmental
sensing, and information exchange in the aircraft, which inte-
grates the core components and key systems that are required
for the aircraft operation.
• Core Components: Various components perform unique
functions to ensure system stability. Specifically, aviation
relays manage the switching of low-power circuits for
the safety of the electrical system [58]. Moreover, engine
ignition systems trigger combustion, which affects engine
efficiency [59]. In addition, circuit protection devices
monitor and disconnect faulty circuits to prevent damage,
and the aviation contactors control the high-power loads
for critical equipment stability [60].
• Key Systems: The power system provides strong thrust
for flight. For example, small and medium engines
are compact and powerful for frequent takeoffs tasks.
Moreover, the hybrid systems [61] offer endurance and
quick response for extended flights, and the onboard
systems support real-time data exchange and path plan-
ning through sensing and navigation. In addition, the
flight control systems can manage the attitude and task
commands to enhance autonomy and adaptability [62].
It is worth noting that the key materials for low-altitude
aircraft are integral to the development of airborne termi-
nals and aircraft manufacturing [72]. In particular, aluminum
alloys, known for their high strength-to-weight ratio and strong
corrosion resistance, are widely used in aircraft structures,
including fixed-wing and helicopters. UAVs are ideal for using
carbon fiber due to its high strength and low density. Moreover,
composite materials enable the lightweight and optimized the
designs for flying cars, such as eVTOLs.
Physical Infrastructure: A comprehensive and well-
rounded operational support system is established to meet
the diverse business needs of enterprises. Specifically, such
a system includes both basic and enhanced facilities, which
not only can support routine operations but also significantly
improve the ability of system to respond quickly to unexpected
situations and environmental changes.
• Basic Facilities: Takeoff and landing stations are crucial
to initiating and completing flight tasks [73]. Trans-
fer facilities enable smooth transitions between takeoff
points and task areas [74]. Moreover, energy stations
provide charging or battery replacement services, while

Low-Altitude Supervision System: The system links mil-
itary and civil aviation regulatory agencies with government
management platforms, which focus on airspace policy for-
mulation, regulatory enforcement, and compliance oversight.
Specifically, the core roles of such systems include real-time
monitoring of airspace activity, evaluating the compliance
of flight operations, and ensuring airspace safety and order
via effective management. Based on this, the system mainly
consists of two key modules:
• Identity Authentication: Digital certificates, biometrics,
and aircraft codes are used to verify the identity of
the aircraft and its crew. Moreover, the system cross-
references databases to confirm qualifications and ensure
compliance with airworthiness standards [71]. Only the
certified aircraft and personnel are granted takeoff clear-
ance, thus preventing illegal flights from the outset.
• Violation Handling: Illegal flights are met with swift
legal action, including thorough investigation, evidence
collection, and penalties ranging from fines to license
suspension or even aircraft confiscation [76]. Moreover,
violations are made public to deter others and uphold the
integrity of low-altitude airspace.
Low-Altitude Flight Service System: The system is
responsible for the overall organization and coordination of
low-altitude aircraft tasks at the planning and management
stage. Specifically, system-level strategies and adaptive plan-
ning mechanisms are applied to ensure efficiency, stability,
and responsiveness in supporting subsequent task execution,
thereby establishing a solid foundation for successful task
completion. The system consists of two main modules:
• Task Scheduling: This process focuses on the dynamic
assignment of tasks to aircraft and the determination
of their execution sequences based on real-time factors
such as task urgency, spatial distribution, and platform
constraints (e.g., battery level or payload capacity). These
strategies aim to enhance responsiveness, balance opera-
tional load, and prevent system bottlenecks [77], [78].
• Resource Coordination: This function manages the
deployment and redistribution of aircraft, energy supplies,
and support infrastructure. Through intelligent forecast-
ing [79] and cross-departmental resource sharing [80], the
module ensures timely availability of essential resources.
Such coordination reduces redundant allocations and
improves resilience under fluctuating task demands.
Low-Altitude Flight Control System: The system exercises
direct control over aircraft during task execution. In dynamic
low-altitude environments, flight control is achieved through
continuous state monitoring, proactive conflict and obstacle
detection, and the issuance of in-flight adjustment commands
to maintain safe navigation and ensure task reliability. The
system is structured around two essential components:
• Trajectory Optimization: This generates efficient flight
trajectories by adjusting parameters such as altitude,
heading, and waypoint timing in response to operational
constraints and environmental conditions [81]. The goal is
to minimize flight duration, reduce energy consumption,
or maximize task coverage, thus supporting optimal in-air
task performance [82].
• Obstacle Avoidance: As a core safety function, this
enables aircraft to detect obstacles such as buildings,
terrain, or nearby aircraft through onboard sensing [83].
Subsequently, the aircraft perform timely and localized
path adjustments in response to these threats, thereby
maintaining safe separation while ensuring efficient and
stable task execution.
C. Key Findings and Insights
Based on the above content, it can be concluded that LAE
networks are built upon a multi-layered architecture sup-
ported by advanced standards, intelligent systems, and robust
infrastructure to enable scalable, autonomous, and reliable
UAV operations in low-altitude airspace. In the following,
we outline key issues that require further research.
• Modular Design: A core trend in LAE networks is the
rise of modular platforms that enable low-altitude aircraft
to switch task functions rapidly without full system
reconfiguration. Compared to traditional tightly coupled
architectures, modern platforms decouple task payloads
such as sensors, communication units, or control modules
into pluggable components [84]. This enables in-flight
reconfiguration based on real-time needs, which supports
efficient adaptation to scenarios such as patrol, logistics,
or emergency response. As this paradigm grows, stan-
dardized interfaces and blockchain-based management
help ensure secure integration, regulatory compliance,
and component traceability [85].
• Edge Intelligence: Another key insight lies in the tran-
sition from centralized cloud computing to onboard AI
deployment in low-altitude aircraft. In bandwidth-limited
or interference-prone environments, real-time decisions
must be made locally. To address this, LAE systems
embed lightweight AI models for core functions such
as local sensing, flight behavior adjustment, and col-
lision avoidance, greatly reducing latency and external
dependence [86]. These models use neural architecture
search and quantization to fit edge devices, while fed-
erated learning allows aircraft to improve local models
collaboratively without sharing raw data [87].
• Infrastructure Awareness: Traditional routing algorithms
for low-altitude aircraft often focus on minimizing dis-
tance or energy use while overlooking the role of critical
ground infrastructure, such as charging stations, main-
tenance hubs, and emergency landing zones. In dense
operational environments, routing must adapt to airspace
dynamics and infrastructure constraints. Through DT
integration of ground facilities, routing plans can dynami-
cally account for real-time loads and queuing delays [88].
This enables a shift from isolated aerial optimization to
system-level coordination that improves resilience and
resource efficiency.

path adjustments in response to these threats, thereby
maintaining safe separation while ensuring efficient and
stable task execution.
C. Key Findings and Insights
Based on the above content, it can be concluded that LAE
networks are built upon a multi-layered architecture sup-
ported by advanced standards, intelligent systems, and robust
infrastructure to enable scalable, autonomous, and reliable
UAV operations in low-altitude airspace. In the following,
we outline key issues that require further research.
• Modular Design: A core trend in LAE networks is the
rise of modular platforms that enable low-altitude aircraft
to switch task functions rapidly without full system
reconfiguration. Compared to traditional tightly coupled
architectures, modern platforms decouple task payloads
such as sensors, communication units, or control modules
into pluggable components [84]. This enables in-flight
reconfiguration based on real-time needs, which supports
efficient adaptation to scenarios such as patrol, logistics,
or emergency response. As this paradigm grows, stan-
dardized interfaces and blockchain-based management
help ensure secure integration, regulatory compliance,
and component traceability [85].
• Edge Intelligence: Another key insight lies in the tran-
sition from centralized cloud computing to onboard AI
deployment in low-altitude aircraft. In bandwidth-limited
or interference-prone environments, real-time decisions
must be made locally. To address this, LAE systems
embed lightweight AI models for core functions such
as local sensing, flight behavior adjustment, and col-
lision avoidance, greatly reducing latency and external
dependence [86]. These models use neural architecture
search and quantization to fit edge devices, while fed-
erated learning allows aircraft to improve local models
collaboratively without sharing raw data [87].
• Infrastructure Awareness: Traditional routing algorithms
for low-altitude aircraft often focus on minimizing dis-
tance or energy use while overlooking the role of critical
ground infrastructure, such as charging stations, main-
tenance hubs, and emergency landing zones. In dense
operational environments, routing must adapt to airspace
dynamics and infrastructure constraints. Through DT
integration of ground facilities, routing plans can dynami-
cally account for real-time loads and queuing delays [88].
This enables a shift from isolated aerial optimization to
system-level coordination that improves resilience and
resource efficiency.
• Context Adaptation: Effective task execution in LAE
networks requires aircraft to understand and adapt to
context such as weather shifts, population density, and
regulatory changes. To adapt accordingly, instead of
reacting passively, aircraft equipped with semantic mod-
eling and rule-based reasoning can revise task priorities
and update planned trajectories in response to current
constraints [89]. By combining geographic data, time
factors, and airspace policies into lightweight inference
engines, aircraft gain the ability to adapt strategies in real
time. Therefore, this context-aware capability supports
safer and more intelligent responses to dynamic airspace.
• Explainable Autonomy: As LAE networks expand into
urban and policy-sensitive areas, system transparency is
essential for earning trust from operators, regulators, and
the public. Aircraft must perform safely and provide
understandable justifications for their actions. Explainable
autonomy frameworks enable human observers to inter-
pret the logic behind aircraft behavior through interfaces
that visualize decision factors [90]. These explanations
enhance accountability and strengthen the credibility of
automated operations, particularly in environments that
demand social oversight and regulatory compliance.

This integration provides essential technical capabilities for

needs, 5G-A [91] has emerged as an enhancement and expan-

such as real-time broadband communication (RTBC), uplink
centric broadband communication (uCBC), and harmonized
communication and sensing (HCS) [92]. These technologies
can effectively support high-demand applications, including
massive IoT [93], autonomous driving [94], and industrial
automation [95].
In the 5G-A technological architecture, millimeter-wave

resources, thereby significantly boosting network capacity and
data transmission rates [99].

path assumptions and omits multi-cell interference. To improve
practical performance, the authors proposed a practical opti-
mization framework for uplink mmWave MIMO-NOMA,

often observed under low SNR conditions, which cannot

task-driven applications, [111] designed an adaptive semantic
communication framework that transmits only task-oriented
features, so that performance in object detection and instance
segmentation is improved. In addition, [112] focused on

architecture, which results in up to 69% improvement in PSNR

loss, leading to more stable communication signals, which is
especially suitable for low-altitude aircraft operating across
wide areas. To fully leverage the potential of LEO satellites,
several innovative technical solutions have been proposed.
For instance, the LEO satellite selection-based computation
offloading algorithm achieved an average total delay of
42.76 ms and improved resource utilization to 66.67% through

ment approach improved the success rate of random access
and reduced power consumption [115], significantly boosting
the performance of Narrowband IoT in LEO satellite net-
works. This approach also reduces the performance gap by
approximately 58% compared to the traditional 3GPP model.

2) Integrated-Active and Passive Sensing: Sensing tech-
nologies gradually evolve toward the integration of collabora-
tive active sensing and non-collaborative passive sensing [120].
· Collaborative Active Sensing: On the one hand, collabo-
rative active sensing relies on the cooperation of multi-modal
sensing technologies, which integrate various sensors, such
as radar, LiDAR, vision, and infrared to comprehensively
perceive the environment from multiple dimensions. The
complementarity of these sensors overcomes the limita-
tions of individual sensors [121], [122], which significantly
improves the sensing accuracy and enhances target detec-
tion, recognition, and tracking precision. For example, the
authors designed a feature registration and complementary
sensing network (FRCPNet) [123], which aligns multi-level
features at the pixel level and enhances the semantic cor-
relation between modalities, thereby improving the accuracy
of salient object detection in combined RGB and thermal
images. Moreover, in [124], a visual transformer-based model
(ViTAL-TAPE) that combines photometric and radiomet-
ric data was introduced to overcome the limitations under
varying lighting and viewing conditions, ultimately achiev-
ing high-precision landing detection with an accuracy of
0.01 meters.
On the other hand, collaborative active sensing benefits
from integrating sensing and communication to enhance both
the accuracy and timeliness of environmental perception.
In this scheme, active sensing collects real-time data, which
is efficiently shared via communication to improve system
responsiveness. For instance, in [125], the authors proposed a
joint sensing-communication UAV network that synchronizes
radar sensing and data communication through beam sharing
to strengthen the collaborative sensing capacity. In another
study [126], the authors combined secondary surveillance
radar with transponder-equipped air obstacles to enable high-
risk target identification with 0.997 accuracy within a 10 km
range by sharing altitude and identification code information.
Furthermore, ISAC is emerging as a key approach, aim-
ing to simultaneously achieve high-efficiency communication
and high-precision sensing within shared spectrum resources.
To support this vision, GAI offers promising solutions with its
powerful capabilities in data modeling, inference, and gener-
ation. Specifically, the authors in [127] proposed a diffusion
model-based direction-of-arrival estimation method for ISAC,
which achieves a mean square error of just 1.03 degrees
under near-field conditions. Moreover, [128] applied condi-
tional GANs to channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent
surface (RIS)-assisted ISAC systems, so that modeling pre-
cision and training efficiency were improved. However, the
generalization capability under dynamic RIS configurations
or non-stationary channels still requires further investiga-
tion. In addition, a secure sensing framework for ISAC was
introduced in [129], which combines discrete and contin-
uous diffusion models to generate safeguarding signals for
authorized devices, thereby reducing the sensing accuracy of
unauthorized devices by approximately 70%. Nevertheless, the
computational overhead introduced by dual diffusion models
may hinder their real-time deployment in resource-constrained
edge environments.
· Non-Collaborative Passive Sensing: Non-collaborative
passive sensing involves utilizing existing wireless commu-
nication signals (e.g., Wi-Fi or 4G/5G signals) to detect the
surrounding environment. Unlike active radar, passive sensing
captures reflected waves from signals emitted by wireless
communication systems to gather environmental information,
without the need for dedicated transmission signals [130]. The
main advantage of this technology is that it does not interfere
with existing communication systems and requires no addi-
tional hardware, which makes it ideal for privacy-preserving
and cost-effective monitoring applications [131]. However,
weak reflected signals in passive sensing are susceptible
to multi-path effects, static clutter, and noise. Additionally,
extracting useful information from these complex signals and
accurately detecting moving targets without active control
remains a challenge.
Consequently, the integration of active and passive sensing
will become the core of intelligent sensing systems. By com-
plementing each other, the system can leverage active radar
for high-precision distance and velocity data, while also using
the environmental changes detected by passive sensing to form
a richer and more accurate perception. For example, in LAE
applications, active radar measures real-time distance between
UAVs and other aircraft, thus providing precise flight trajectory
information, while passive sensing aids in detecting and track-
ing surrounding ground targets, such as vehicles or buildings.
This collaboration not only improves the perception accuracy
and robustness, but also optimizes the resource utilization.
However, fully exploiting the benefits of this collaboration
requires overcoming challenges such as signal interference,
real-time system coordination, and multi-modal data fusion.

collaboration [132]. However, it faces several challenges
when applied to large-scale scenarios. These include difficulty
handling unpredictable environments, increased latency when
processing large data volumes, and loss of key information
during high-dimensional feature extraction. To address these
issues, GAI has emerged as a promising solution to improve
decision-making in LAE networks.

its powerful modeling and contextual reasoning capabilities

operations in dynamic environments, as shown in Fig. 3

2) Integrated-Active and Passive Sensing: Sensing tech-
nologies gradually evolve toward the integration of collabora-
tive active sensing and non-collaborative passive sensing [120].
· Collaborative Active Sensing: On the one hand, collabo-
rative active sensing relies on the cooperation of multi-modal
sensing technologies, which integrate various sensors, such
as radar, LiDAR, vision, and infrared to comprehensively
perceive the environment from multiple dimensions. The
complementarity of these sensors overcomes the limita-
tions of individual sensors [121], [122], which significantly
improves the sensing accuracy and enhances target detec-
tion, recognition, and tracking precision. For example, the
authors designed a feature registration and complementary
sensing network (FRCPNet) [123], which aligns multi-level
features at the pixel level and enhances the semantic cor-
relation between modalities, thereby improving the accuracy
of salient object detection in combined RGB and thermal
images. Moreover, in [124], a visual transformer-based model
(ViTAL-TAPE) that combines photometric and radiomet-
ric data was introduced to overcome the limitations under
varying lighting and viewing conditions, ultimately achiev-
ing high-precision landing detection with an accuracy of
0.01 meters.
On the other hand, collaborative active sensing benefits
from integrating sensing and communication to enhance both
the accuracy and timeliness of environmental perception.
In this scheme, active sensing collects real-time data, which
is efficiently shared via communication to improve system
responsiveness. For instance, in [125], the authors proposed a
joint sensing-communication UAV network that synchronizes
radar sensing and data communication through beam sharing
to strengthen the collaborative sensing capacity. In another
study [126], the authors combined secondary surveillance
radar with transponder-equipped air obstacles to enable high-
risk target identification with 0.997 accuracy within a 10 km
range by sharing altitude and identification code information.
Furthermore, ISAC is emerging as a key approach, aim-
ing to simultaneously achieve high-efficiency communication
and high-precision sensing within shared spectrum resources.
To support this vision, GAI offers promising solutions with its
powerful capabilities in data modeling, inference, and gener-
ation. Specifically, the authors in [127] proposed a diffusion
model-based direction-of-arrival estimation method for ISAC,
which achieves a mean square error of just 1.03 degrees
under near-field conditions. Moreover, [128] applied condi-
tional GANs to channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent
surface (RIS)-assisted ISAC systems, so that modeling pre-
cision and training efficiency were improved. However, the
generalization capability under dynamic RIS configurations
or non-stationary channels still requires further investiga-
tion. In addition, a secure sensing framework for ISAC was
introduced in [129], which combines discrete and contin-
uous diffusion models to generate safeguarding signals for
authorized devices, thereby reducing the sensing accuracy of
unauthorized devices by approximately 70%. Nevertheless, the
computational overhead introduced by dual diffusion models
may hinder their real-time deployment in resource-constrained
edge environments.
· Non-Collaborative Passive Sensing: Non-collaborative
passive sensing involves utilizing existing wireless commu-
nication signals (e.g., Wi-Fi or 4G/5G signals) to detect the
surrounding environment. Unlike active radar, passive sensing
captures reflected waves from signals emitted by wireless
communication systems to gather environmental information,
without the need for dedicated transmission signals [130]. The
main advantage of this technology is that it does not interfere
with existing communication systems and requires no addi-
tional hardware, which makes it ideal for privacy-preserving
and cost-effective monitoring applications [131]. However,
weak reflected signals in passive sensing are susceptible
to multi-path effects, static clutter, and noise. Additionally,
extracting useful information from these complex signals and
accurately detecting moving targets without active control
remains a challenge.
Consequently, the integration of active and passive sensing
will become the core of intelligent sensing systems. By com-
plementing each other, the system can leverage active radar
for high-precision distance and velocity data, while also using
the environmental changes detected by passive sensing to form
a richer and more accurate perception. For example, in LAE
applications, active radar measures real-time distance between
UAVs and other aircraft, thus providing precise flight trajectory
information, while passive sensing aids in detecting and track-
ing surrounding ground targets, such as vehicles or buildings.
This collaboration not only improves the perception accuracy
and robustness, but also optimizes the resource utilization.
However, fully exploiting the benefits of this collaboration
requires overcoming challenges such as signal interference,
real-time system coordination, and multi-modal data fusion.

during high-dimensional feature extraction. To address these
issues, GAI has emerged as a promising solution to improve
decision-making in LAE networks.

have emerged as another key paradigm of GAI in LAE
networks. Specifically, prompt engineering offers a lightweight
solution that requires no modification of the model parame-

and demonstrations, so that the model can fully activate its
existing knowledge and reasoning capabilities to accomplish
complex tasks. For instance, the in-context learning (ICL)
approach [140] allows a model to utilize historical network
configurations or optimization strategies as contextual input.

enhances intermediate reasoning transparency, which supports
logically demanding tasks without increasing inference cost.

in emergency scenarios. In the ICL-based data collection

natural language task descriptions and delivered to the LLM,
which generates updated scheduling strategies based on the
current context. Once the strategy is executed, performance
feedback, such as packet loss, is incorporated into the task
description. This updated context serves as the basis for the
next inference cycle, allowing the system to refine its decisions
over time and respond effectively to evolving environmental
conditions. As such, this closed-loop mechanism enhances
operational robustness and makes the ICL particularly suitable
for low-altitude UAV systems operating under constrained
communication and limited computational resources.

ability to handle complex tasks, which enables effective
support for multi-stage reasoning and autonomous decision-
making. This capability aligns well with the characteristics
of LAE networks, where task dependencies often involve
multiple variables and layered processes. Specifically, the
chain-of-thought prompting technique [140] guides the model
to explicitly present intermediate reasoning steps in a progres-
sive manner, so that the logical clarity and problem-solving
ability are significantly enhanced. In addition, the prompt-
based planning strategy [140] allows large-scale network
operations to be broken down into a series of manageable
subtasks, which fits scenarios that require sequential execution
such as network planning, deployment, and dynamic recon-
figuration. Beyond this, the self-refinement mechanism [140]
permits the model to generate feedback from its own outputs
and revise prompts iteratively without human intervention.

an effective solution for LAE wireless systems that require
real-time adaptation and continuous learning, while highlight-

system intelligence and long-term sustainability.

task scenarios, training protocols, and simulated environments,

realism. In addition, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

agents perform subtasks such as target identification, route

This collaboration forms the foundation for flight stability
and precise operations in the LAE networks. Positioning
ensures accurate location tracking in complex environments,

continuously monitors the airspace, thus identifying potential
risks in real time. The coordination of these technologies
greatly increases the situational awareness of the aircraft and
reinforces the safety defenses of the system.

3) Real-Time Surveillance: Automatic dependent
surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) is a data broadcast-based
air traffic surveillance technology, which is designed for
real-time monitoring and collision avoidance of low-altitude
aircraft [187]. To be specific, ADS-B enables aircraft to
periodically broadcast position, speed, heading, altitude, and
other data via an onboard transmitter. This information is
transmitted through radio frequencies and can be received
by other aircraft and ground control stations, thereby
allowing real-time tracking of the aircraft. Unlike traditional
surveillance methods that rely on radar echoes [188], ADS-B
provides precise location data based on the GNSS, with the
ability to automatically broadcast, which offers advantages
in terms of accuracy and timeliness. In addition, ADS-B
features high precision, low latency, and wide coverage,
so that it can offer reliable surveillance services over large
areas. This makes it particularly suitable for complex low-
altitude airspace, so that significantly improving the air traffic
management efficiency and enhancing aircraft safety. Based
on these advantages, [189] developed a conflict awareness
scheme for UAVs that analyzes the ADS-B message flow and
format to identify potential conflicts. Next, strategies, such
as speed adjustments and direction changes, based on the
unscented Kalman filter were applied to resolve conflicts. This
approach significantly improves the UAV conflict resolution
capabilities, and provides a strong theoretical foundation
for the advancement of collision avoidance technologies in
UAVs.

improving the ability of the system to guard against GNSS
spoofing. However, these techniques require high data quality
and computational resources, and in certain complex signal
scenarios or cases with significant data discrepancies, the
accuracy and generalization ability of the model may be
compromised.
Beyond security concerns, the deployment challenges and
adaptation issues of ADS-B in low-altitude environments also
deserve attention. Specifically, regarding the challenges, the
sharp increase in aerial vehicle density, particularly with the
proliferation of UAVs and eVTOL aircraft, may lead to broad-
cast congestion and channel collisions. Unlike well-spaced
high-altitude flights, low-altitude traffic tends to be dense and
dynamic, which can make it challenging for ADS-B to main-
tain stable communication due to frequent interference [203].
Moreover, complex urban or mountainous environments often
introduce signal occlusion and multipath effects, thereby
resulting in intermittent reception or localization errors that
may reduce the reliability of GNSS-based positioning. Fur-
thermore, LAE platforms typically experience rapid mobility
and frequent topological changes, which may not align well
with the static periodic broadcast mechanism of ADS-B [204].
In terms of adaptability, ADS-B was originally designed
for crewed aviation, which assumes standardized hardware,
ample power supply, and relatively stable flight patterns.
In contrast, LAE networks comprise highly heterogeneous
and resource-constrained platforms, where limitations in size,
weight, and power may restrict the integration of conventional
ADS-B modules [205]. Additionally, ADS-B lacks adaptive
features such as dynamic broadcast intervals or priority-based
message scheduling, which may limit its responsiveness in
decentralized and bursty communication environments. There-
fore, effective deployment in LAE scenarios may require not
only protocol-level improvements but also reconsideration of
key design assumptions to better accommodate lightweight,
autonomous, and decentralized operations.

This fusion is crucial for improving the efficiency and
safety of low-altitude airspace operations. Flight control opti-
mizes flight paths through intelligent scheduling to ensure
smooth operations in high-density airspace, while airspace

1) Advanced-Flight Control: Proportional integral differen-
tial (PID) control [209] is one of the most common traditional
flight control approaches. This method maintains aircraft sta-
bility by adjusting control inputs based on real-time feedback
of attitude and position [210]. However, traditional PID control
often struggles to address the challenges posed by nonlinear
systems, external disturbances, and parameter tuning when
faced with complex and dynamic flight tasks, thus limiting its
performance. Moreover, model predictive control (MPC) rep-
resents another advanced flight control method that predicts the
future state of an aircraft and generates control inputs through
optimization to achieve optimal decision-making [211]. Unlike
PID control, which focuses on current errors, MPC also
considers changes in future states and constraints. For instance,
the authors in [212] proposed a general-model dynamic formu-
lation and a two-layered constrained MPC strategy to tackle
the trajectory tracking problem for tilt-rotor UAVs. Moreover,
a novel nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) approach
was designed to address UAV navigation and obstacle avoid-
ance [213]. While these methods perform well in trajectory
tracking and obstacle avoidance tasks, there remains room
for improvement in terms of state prediction accuracy and
optimization of control decisions. Building on these limita-
tions, AI-based low-level flight control and human-in-the-loop
reinforcement learning (HITL-RL)-driven high-level decision-
making and coordination strategies have become increasingly
essential.
· AI-based PID: Adopting AI-based PID control enhances
the adaptability and robustness of the system in complex
environments. For example, [214] improved traditional PID
by integrating a feedforward neural network, which main-
tains the stability of the quadrotor while addressing hardware
limitations and enhancing control accuracy. However, as AI
advances, relying solely on PID is inadequate for complex
tasks involving external disturbances and internal uncer-
tainties. To address this, a robust intelligent self-adjusting
propulsion control approach has emerged. For instance, the
authors in [215] developed a hybrid control approach com-
bining PID and intelligent active force control (IAFC) to
enhance the disturbance rejection capability and agility per-
formance of a quadrotor UAV. To further enhance robustness,
an AI-based iterative learning algorithm (ILAFC) was used
to automatically adjust control parameters (Fig. 8), which
results in a 17% improvement in disturbance rejection and
agility performance. In addition to optimizing the control
strategy, the computational bottleneck faced by the aircraft
during target detection and tracking tasks also needs to be
addressed. For example, [216] introduced a heterogeneous
parallelization strategy that integrates target detection and
tracking algorithms with UAV control software. Then, based
on target tracking data, a gain-scheduled PID controller further
optimizes flight control to ensure efficient task execution

spans.content: In summary, the fusion of flight control and airspace man-
agement plays a critical role in improving the safety and
efficiency of low-altitude airspace operations. While the key
technologies required for each have been outlined in Table VII,
existing research has yet to explore the comprehensive fusion.
In response to this gap, recent studies have shown that integrat-
ing GAI with communication, navigation, and flight control
empowers UAV systems with more efficient path planning,
greater operational safety, and smoother trajectory generation.
For instance, generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL)
was applied to virtual navigation training to imitate expert
trajectories [232], which improves UAV path planning and
generalization in complex 3D environments. Building on this,
a multi-agent PPO-based GAIL framework with parallel sam-
pling was proposed, which boosts the target discovery rate to
73.33% in cooperative UAV search tasks, while increasing the
average system cost by only 1.11% [233], thus achieving an
effective trade-off between efficiency and safety. In addition,
the BezierVAE architecture was designed to extend TrajVAE
by introducing a Bezier curve output layer [234], which
improves trajectory smoothness in both spatial and velocity
domains, reduces reconstruction error by 91.3%, and lowers
trajectory roughness by 83.4%, thereby demonstrating stronger
generalization and greater adaptability to safety verification
tasks.
Moreover, leveraging GAI across computing, communi-
cation/flight control, and airspace management technologies
facilitates robust resource coordination and system stabil-
ity in LAE environments. For example, [235] introduced a
Lyapunov-based mechanism that integrates GDM with RL,
so that the system maintains long-term stability and achieves
efficient resource allocation under conflicting objectives and
external disturbances. Furthermore, in [236], the authors
developed a GDM-based multi-agent DDPG algorithm that
incorporates the Hungarian algorithm (HG-MADDPG), thus
achieving up to 20.35% reduction in average task completion
latency under dynamic resource conditions. However, a lack
of dynamic network topology consideration may limit the
performance of the system in complex environments. In addi-
tion, in heterogeneous and service-diverse RIS scenarios, the
authors combined GAI with distributed reinforcement learning
(DBRL) to design an on-demand scheduling mechanism [237],
which maintains a stable quality of service satisfaction rate
(QoSSR) around 1.0 even under limited bandwidth in vir-
tual reality video scenarios. Collectively, these developments
underscore the necessity of further exploring GAI-enabled
fusion to advance intelligent coordination and operational
resilience within LAE networks.

narios (Fig. 13) address long-term and system-level airspace
operations. In addition, inspection scenarios (Fig. 14) focus on

ing, and public safety monitoring. Moreover, we present pilot
deployments that correspond to these scenarios.

a residential building), the goal is to quickly and efficiently
complete the “last-mile” [243], which ensures that the UAVs
reach their destination precisely and safely within a small
area. In particular, GNSS signals are typically stable enough
to provide global positioning support, and 5G-A or Wi-Fi
networks are sufficient to support real-time data transmission
and command updates. The focus shifts to more precise
environmental awareness and flight control. For instance,
in urban or residential areas, UAVs face numerous dynamic
obstacles, such as pedestrians, vehicles, and buildings [244].
To avoid collisions, SLAM continuously updates maps using
camera data [245], while infrared sensors detect non-visible
obstacles in low-light or foggy conditions [246]. In addition,
to improve adaptability, GAI-integrated SLAM systems apply
learned priors so that occluded scenes can be reconstructed
and motion trends of dynamic obstacles can be predicted,
which enhances collision avoidance and trajectory planning.

instructions (e.g., “avoid school zone or land on rooftop”)
through LLMs, thereby enabling adaptive task adjustment
without human reprogramming. This allows the UAVs to
update policies based on environmental feedback and semantic
constraints in real time.
B. Low-Altitude Rescue
The key to this application lies in rapid response, precise
positioning, and environmental awareness, which guarantees
the UAVs can quickly reach target areas and execute tasks
in emergency situations. To be specific, 5G-A and LEO
satellite communications provide reliable communication links
between UAVs and rescue command centers [247]. This
ensures that the UAVs can receive instructions and transmit
data continuously in complex or remote rescue scenarios.
This is crucial for real-time tracking of rescue progress
and sharing on-site information, such as video streams and
environmental data. Moreover, infrared sensors and LiDAR
offer precise environmental perception in low-light or harsh
weather conditions, thereby enabling the detection of potential
obstacles, assessment of disaster-affected areas, and identifi-
cation of rescue targets. For example, infrared sensors detect
heat sources [248], such as the body temperature of trapped
individuals, to locate survivors or hot spots, so that the UAVs
can identify targets in low-light or poor-visibility conditions.
In addition, LiDAR provides 3D mapping of disaster zones
to help rescue teams plan operations [249]. To enhance
autonomous perception under such conditions, GAI models are
deployed at the edge, where compressed multi-modal networks
infer semantic information from limited sensor input. For
instance, GDMs can generate structured 3D maps from sparse
data, thus improving the identification of viable paths and
likely human figures even in partially observed or degraded
environments.

E. Pilot Deployments Across Scenarios
Low-altitude aerial mobility is gradually moving beyond
conceptual studies, with pilot deployments beginning to
emerge in logistics, rescue, transportation, and inspection.
Specifically, in logistics, EHang deployed autonomous aerial
vehicles in Shenzhen to deliver emergency supplies.4 More-
over, in the United States, Zipline received approval from
the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to conduct rou-
tine BVLOS UAV deliveries, which enables scalable medical
logistics without the need for visual observers.5 For res-
cue, SoftBank used tethered UAVs to restore communication
after the Noto earthquake,6 while the Japan UAS Industrial
Development Association (JUIDA) coordinated UAV tasks
for search and delivery.7 In transportation, EHang conducted
public demonstration flights of the EH216-S at the urban air
mobility (UAM) operation demonstration center in Shenzhen.8
Moreover, Joby Aviation and the National Aeronautics and
Space Administration (NASA) carried out high-fidelity simu-
lations in the Dallas–Fort Worth area to validate the feasibility
of managing more than 100 eVTOL operations per hour
using advanced air traffic systems.9 In addition, South Korea
integrates vertiport design, air corridor planning, and multi-
party test flights to support commercial service readiness by
2025.10 In inspection, JOUAV deployed the CW-15 VTOL
UAV with JoLiDAR-1000 to inspect 33.7 km of high-voltage
power lines across the karst terrain in Guangxi Province,
China.11 In addition, the United Kingdom received one of
the first routine BVLOS permissions to autonomously inspect
transmission towers using LIDAR and panoramic sensors.12
Collectively, these deployments reflect the early-stage but
expanding application of low-altitude aerial systems in diverse
real-world contexts.

analysis with semantic mapping [263]. For example,
using shadow fragments, edge cues, and motion patterns,

require simulated training and continuous adaptation to
stay reliable under degraded sensing.

urgency, location, and semantic input [236]. When dis-

decentralized cooperation and adaptive task handoff.

V. FUTURE DIRECTIONS
In this section, we will present important future directions
for collaborative technologies in LAE networks.
A. Intelligent and Adaptive Optimization of Dynamic
Airspace
The coexistence of high-density, multi-type aircraft in
low-altitude airspace requires overcoming traditional air traf-
fic control constraints by establishing an intelligent and
adaptive management system. By integrating GAI-enabled
DRL [266], game theory [267], and DT systems [134]
alongside various low-altitude sensors and communication
devices, the system can predict environmental changes, model
task dynamics, and optimize control strategies. In addition,
establishing cross-domain transfer learning mechanisms would
enable the efficient reuse of GDM-generated synthetic DT
data across heterogeneous low-altitude aircraft platforms, thus
reducing reliance on real-world samples while enhancing
model generalization and deployment efficiency. Moreover,
airspace usage rights can be managed through an auction
model [268] that incorporates different time slots and priority
tasks to design differentiated pricing strategies. Furthermore,
blockchain smart contracts [269] can then be used to automat-
ically execute transactions, thus incentivizing users to actively
avoid peak airspace and optimizing flight management within
the LAE networks.
B. Security and Privacy Protection of LAE Networks
The openness and data mobility of LAE networks expose
them to multiple security threats, which necessitate a multi-
layered defense system. For example, the cloud-edge-end
collaborative security architecture can protect data con-
fidentiality and integrity by deploying trusted execution
environments (TEEs) on aircraft [270], running intrusion
detection systems (IDS) at edge nodes [271], and utilizing
homomorphic encryption at the cloud level [272]. In terms
of the privacy protection, LAE networks involve substantial
amounts of user data (e.g., flight trajectories and personal iden-
tities). Therefore, techniques such as differential privacy [273]
and federated learning [274] can anonymize and protect user
data, thus ensuring that the privacy is not compromised during
data sharing and analysis. To further enhance the security and
privacy, network resilience is required to handle unexpected
events such as cyberattacks or equipment failures. Thus, AI-
based anomaly detection [275], autonomous reconfiguration
mechanisms [276], and multi-path communication technolo-
gies [277] can be employed to improve system adaptability and
recovery capabilities, so that continuous protection of critical
data and services is ensured.
C. Sustainable Power and Energy Management of Aircraft
The development of LAE networks may face challenges
in sustainable energy supply, particularly with the large-
scale deployment of high-energy-consuming aircraft such as
eVTOLs and UAVs, which require the enhanced dynamic
response and sustainability in energy systems. Future research
can focus on aerial energy relay networks [278], where solar-
powered UAVs function as the charging stations to create an
air-to-air energy supply chain. Furthermore, bio-hybrid energy
systems could be explored [279], which use microbial fuel
cells along with rainwater and carbon dioxide collected from
aircraft surfaces to generate power. MmWave beamforming
and laser energy transmission [280] could enable wireless
charging of aircraft during hovering or low-speed cruising.
In addition, energy consumption prediction models that couple
flight tasks, weather conditions, and battery health status could
be developed, with GAI-enabled DRL used to optimize power
distribution [281].
D. Quantum-Driven Intelligence Coordination for Airspace
As LAE networks evolve toward massive-scale aircraft
coordination in real time, classical computational paradigms
may struggle to handle the exponential growth of state-action
spaces and multi-agent constraints. To address this, integrating
quantum computing, particularly quantum annealing [282] and
variational quantum circuits [283], into airspace management
makes it possible to accelerate route optimization, task allo-
cation, and conflict resolution in high-density low-altitude
environments. In particular, quantum-inspired algorithms can
be embedded into DT platforms to simulate thousands of
parallel flight scenarios under uncertainty [284]. Moreover,
hybrid classical-quantum models can support the optimization
of secure and ultra-fast communication protocols by lever-
aging quantum entanglement properties [285], which in turn
strengthens the resilience of collaborative decision-making
among aircraft clusters in contested or congested airspace.
E. Self-Evolving Cognitive Agents for Generative
Governance
Future research should advance self-evolving cognitive
agents for low-altitude airspace with generative and interactive
capabilities to enhance autonomy, adaptability, and safety. One
promising direction is the fusion of GAI and XR technologies,
which can enable cross-modal semantic alignment of visual,
linguistic, and spatial data in XR environments to enhance
task comprehension and command execution [142]. In par-
allel, the development of lightweight GAI models optimized
for resource-constrained XR-aircraft platforms is essential to
ensure real-time performance and operational stability under
real-world conditions [286]. Another critical avenue is the
incorporation of HITL-RL into multi-agent systems, which has
the potential to support preference-driven policy adjustment,
task reconfiguration, and dynamic risk intervention [219].
By leveraging human feedback to perform localized policy
corrections and knowledge transfer in scenarios with unstable
communication or sudden task changes, the system can enable
a self-evolving airspace architecture characterized by continu-
ous learning, human supervision, and safety assurance.
